title: Three-color triangles mathematical overview
sections: A large triangle is divided into finitely many little triangles meeting only along whole edges or at vertices. Its corners have labels R, B and Y. Every vertex on an outside side may use only that side's two corner labels; interior vertices may use any of the three labels. Count little cells, not larger triangles made from several cells.

Every such labeling has an odd number of little triangles with all three labels, and therefore at least one. This statement is independent of triangle sizes and of the particular subdivision. Allowing a forbidden boundary label can destroy the guarantee.

An R-B edge is a door. A little triangle has zero, one or two doors; it has exactly one precisely when it has R, B and Y. Across the outside boundary there are an odd number of doors: only the R-B side contributes, and its endpoint labels differ. Each interior door is counted twice. Thus the number of one-door cells is odd. In the equivalent path picture, two-door cells pass a route through; components may be paths or closed loops. A chosen outside entrance can return outside, although not all entrances can pair that way.

K-1 moves labels and searches for possible counts and locations, including a changed-boundary example. Grades 2-3 learns doors, local cases and pairing. Grades 4-5 connects boundary parity to all-three cells on any allowed triangulation and tests the boundary hypothesis.

Let children experiment before naming an odd-count conjecture. A complete check of a small board proves only that board; the door count or pairing argument explains every permitted labeling and subdivision. The detailed paths, witnesses and proof follow the preparation pages.
